description: Masoom and Waniya here, two students who love space and games. We built The Final Countdown because we wanted an easier way to see how every decision in a space mission affects everything else. We hope it gets more students curious about how real missions are built.
summary:
THE FINAL COUNTDOWN is a free browser game where 1–4 players design, launch and fly a complete space mission. Players choose one of five science missions (wildfire detection, lunar ice, solar-storm warning, Mars and an infrared observatory). They then move through phases modeled on NASA JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels: objectives, orbit, instruments, spacecraft, launch and ground station. Live gauges show how every choice trades off mass, power, data, communications, budget and time, using real physics such as the rocket equation, orbital mechanics and radio link budgets. A pixel-art astronaut guide explains each decision. Teams vote GO/NO-GO at a Flight Readiness Review, watch the countdown, and then operate their spacecraft through real solar flares and geomagnetic storms pulled live from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. A post-mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed and compares it with real NASA missions.

The challenge asks for a tool that turns abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on experience. Ours runs in any browser with no login, so any student or classroom can experience whole-mission systems engineering and learn by designing, failing and trying again.
details:
The Final Countdown

The title screen. The panel on the left shows live space weather from NASA DONKI.

The problem

Every space mission is a balancing act. If you want a better camera, you need more power to run it and a faster radio to send its pictures home, and suddenly the spacecraft is too heavy for the rocket you can afford. At school these topics are usually taught separately, so students rarely get to see how one decision affects the rest of the mission. We wanted to build something where you feel that for yourself, in a game that takes about 15 minutes.

How it works

  1. Pick a mission. There are five to choose from, each based on real science: spotting wildfires from orbit (Ember Watch), finding ice in the Moon's dark craters (Cold Trap), warning Earth about solar storms (Storm Sentinel), studying where Mars lost its water (Red Horizon) and building an infrared telescope (First Light).
  2. Design the spacecraft. You go through the same stages NASA teams use when they turn an idea into a mission, based on JPL's Concept Maturity Levels and Goddard's Mission Design Lab. You set your goals, then choose an orbit, instruments, the spacecraft's systems, a rocket and a ground station. A dashboard on the side updates as you go, and every option shows you what it would change before you pick it.
  3. Get a GO. Before launch there's a Flight Readiness Review. It lists anything that would stop the mission and explains why. Each team lead then votes GO or NO-GO.
  4. Launch and fly. After the countdown, the rocket's real success rate decides if the launch works. Once you're in space, real solar flares and geomagnetic storms from NASA's DONKI database hit your spacecraft, along with problems like a broken reaction wheel or a piece of debris heading your way. You decide how to respond.
  5. See how you did. At the end you get a score out of 1000 and an explanation of what went right and wrong. The report also tells you which real mission your design is closest to, and you can export your orbit to NASA's GMAT software.

Designing a telescope mission. The dashboard and the spacecraft change with every choice, and Commander Vance gives tips in the corner.

What makes it creative

  • A tiny astronaut guide. Commander Arlo Vance is a little pixel-art astronaut who stays with you the whole time. He gives you tips in a speech bubble, warns you when something won't work, reacts when a solar storm hits and tells you what he thinks of your final grade. It feels like having a mentor next to you instead of reading a manual.
  • Music that changes with the moment. The game makes its own soundtrack in the browser. While you're designing, the music is slow and calm. Once the countdown starts it switches to a faster track with a heavier beat, and it stays that way through launch and the mission.
  • A spacecraft you watch being built. The spacecraft on screen changes every time you make a choice. Choose a bigger body and it grows. Add solar panels, an antenna or a telescope mirror and you see them appear. Your decisions show up as something you can look at, which makes them easier to understand.

The Flight Readiness Review, where each team lead votes GO or NO-GO.

An example from the game

Here is the wildfire mission (Ember Watch) built three different ways:

  • A small CubeSat that rides along on someone else's rocket costs $9.8M but only reaches 34% of the science goals, because its simple camera can't pick up smaller fires.
  • A bigger SmallSat with a cooled infrared sensor and its own small rocket costs $62M out of an $80M budget and reaches 76% of the goals.
  • That same SmallSat fails the review if you forget to plan how it leaves orbit. At 700 km it would stay up for about 40 years, and the rules say it has to come down within 5.

A few other things the game teaches the hard way: a Mars orbiter with no engine can't slow down and flies straight past the planet. An infrared telescope that isn't kept cold loses most of its science (105% drops to 13%). And picking a nuclear power source for a Mars mission can delay it past its launch window, which means waiting 26 months and paying $52M to keep the team going.

There isn't one correct design. Different choices can all work, and each one comes with its own costs, which is how real mission planning works too.

How we use NASA data

  • Live space weather from NASA DONKI. The game downloads the real flares, coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms from the past 60 days and replays them during your mission, so every flight is different. What a storm does depends on your design. It can pull a low satellite down, crash a computer in deep space or give a storm-watching mission extra science. If the connection to NASA fails, the game uses real past storms instead, like the big one in May 2024.
  • The challenge resources shaped how the game works. Concept Maturity Levels gave us the order of the phases. The Mission Design Lab gave us the review checks, and Design and Develop Science Missions helped us split the mission into launch, space, ground and user parts. CubeSat 101 is where our CubeSat sizes and debris rules come from. We also export to GMAT, took ideas from NASA Mission Viz for the orbit view and from the Webb learning game for comparing your design to real missions, and link to the CSA's learning games.
  • Partner agency missions. Missions from ISRO (Chandrayaan-1, Mars Orbiter Mission), ESA (SOHO, Euclid) and the UAE's MBRSC (Emirates Mars Mission) show up as real examples to compare against.
  • Covering the challenge. We tried to include everything the challenge asked for: setting objectives, designing the spacecraft, choosing instruments, picking a rocket and orbit, managing resources, playing alone or in a team of up to four, random events, difficulty levels, a sandbox mode, a dashboard, a leaderboard, saving and sharing designs, and a report at the end.

A real solar particle event, pulled live from NASA DONKI, hitting the spacecraft during a mission.

The science behind it

The numbers in the game come from real physics, simplified so they run in a browser:

  • Fuel uses the rocket equation: mprop = mdry × (eΔv / (Isp × g₀) − 1)
  • Radio speed uses a link budget: rate ≈ P × Gt × Gr × (λ / 4πd)² / (k × T × losses). For a 3 m dish at Mars it gives about 1 Mbps, which is in line with real Mars orbiters.
  • Orbits and eclipses use Kepler's third law with real planet sizes. The game works out the space station's orbit as 92.4 minutes; the real value is 92.6.
  • Solar power gets weaker the farther you are from the Sun (1,361 W/m² at Earth), drops to zero in a planet's shadow and fades a little each year.
  • We also included rocket capacity for each destination, development time based on how proven the technology is, Mars launch windows every 26 months and the 5-year rule for clearing low orbit.
  • Scoring is out of 1000: 400 for science, 200 for mission success, 150 for using resources well, 150 for good decisions and 100 for teamwork.

We wrote 53 automated tests that check these numbers against real values. There is a working reference design for every mission, and we ran 300 random designs through the game to make sure nothing breaks.

The report at the end gives a score out of 1000 and explains what went right and wrong.

Why it's useful

  • It's free and runs in a normal browser on a laptop or phone. Nobody needs an account.
  • A mission fits in one class period, and there are three difficulty levels, from Cadet up to Flight Director.
  • When something goes wrong, the game explains why instead of just marking it as a mistake.
  • In team mode, each player is in charge of one area (science, spacecraft, orbit or ground operations), so they have to talk to each other and agree before they launch.
  • Because the space weather is real and changes, you can fly the same design twice and get a different story. You can also send a friend a link to fly your exact design.

Who it's for and the impact we hope for

We built this for students who might never get to sit in a mission design room. It connects to UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education), because it gives anyone free access to the kind of thinking normally taught at university.

We also kept schools with limited resources in mind. The whole game is about 320 KB, it works on older laptops and phones, and it still runs with saved storm data if the connection to NASA drops. Up to four students can share one computer as a team.

Our hope is that someone plays it, gets curious about how real missions are built and wants to learn more.

Tools we used

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, without any frameworks or outside scripts
  • Canvas and SVG to draw all the pixel art in code
  • The Web Audio API for the sound effects and the music
  • The NASA DONKI API (api.nasa.gov) for space weather
  • Python for our build scripts
  • GitHub and Vercel to host the site, with security headers and a content security policy
  • An AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), which helped write code and text. We reviewed everything and noted this in the project.

Things we kept in mind

  • Accuracy: we checked the game's numbers against real missions with automated tests.
  • Accessibility: simple wording, tooltips for space terms, keyboard controls, an option for reduced motion and a layout that works on phones.
  • Keeping it fun: each mission has a story, and the guide, the music and the growing spacecraft make the process feel alive.
  • Reliability: the game keeps working with saved storm data if NASA's live feed is down.
  • Privacy: there are no accounts, and we don't collect any personal data.
  • Following the rules: everything is in English, there's no NASA branding, all characters are fictional adults, the art and music are our own, and every outside resource is listed in our references.
